one_liner: Header-only C++17 minimal perfect hash library (PTHash/PHOBIC) with 3.1-4.6x faster lookups than BBHash at ~3 bits/key.
what_it_does: Builds a static minimal perfect hash function: given n distinct keys (uint64_t, std::string or std::string_view out of the box), it produces f, which maps each key to a unique slot in [0, n) that you use to index your own value array. You pick a template type (single_phf, partitioned_phf for PTHash-HEM, or dense_partitioned_phf/phobic for PHOBIC) with a hasher, bucketer, encoder and Minimal flag. You then build it with build_in_internal_memory or build_in_external_memory from a key iterator and a build_configuration, and query it with f(key). The API is unlike BBHash's boomphf::mphf, and the built function can be saved, loaded or mmapped through the bundled essentials helpers.
how_it_is_fast: It revisits the FCH (Fox-Chen-Heath) scheme: keys are hashed once into buckets (skewed so 60% of keys land in 30% of buckets, or with PHOBIC's 'optimal' bucket function), and the builder processes buckets largest-first, searching for a small integer 'pilot' per bucket that sends all its keys to free slots via a multiply-high reduction of mix(h(x) XOR mix(pilot)). A lookup is therefore one key hash, one random access into a compressed pilot array and a multiply, whereas BBHash can hash the key several times per lookup (once per level). The pilots compress well because small ones are tried first; encodings include compact, dictionary, Elias-Fano, Rice, front/back 'dual' and PHOBIC's interleaved codes. Building with a load factor alpha < 1 makes the pilot search much faster, and minimality is restored by an Elias-Fano 'free slots' array consulted only for keys that land at a position >= n.
when_to_use: Static sets of millions to billions of keys (64-bit integers, strings, URLs, n-grams) where lookup latency matters most. On 1B random 64-bit keys, a single core looks up in 37-55 ns/key at 3.0-3.2 bits/key.
Build-once/query-many deployments. You build offline, serialize with essentials::save, and load or mmap the function at query time.
Long variable-length keys. PTHash hashes each key only once per lookup; the paper reports only a 6-26 ns/key increase for q-grams and URLs relative to 64-bit keys.
Key sets larger than RAM. single_phf and partitioned_phf have external-memory builders capped by config.ram, and construction can be multi-threaded with config.num_threads.

Space/speed tuning. The author's current recommended default is PHOBIC (dense partitioned, C-int encoder, opt bucketer, lambda=7). On 100M keys with 8 threads on a Xeon W-2245, it gave 2.51 bits/key and 33.5 ns/key lookup in an 8.3 s build (author's own benchmark, with no BBHash comparison).
when_not_to_use: Dynamic key sets. The function is static by design, so any insert or delete means a full rebuild.
When single-threaded build time matters more than lookup speed. At similar space on 1B keys, BBHash gamma=1 built in 253 s versus 689-1042 s for the fast-lookup PTHash configurations.

Tiny key sets (tens to thousands of keys). Fixed metadata dominates: 469 bits/key for 6 keys was reported in issue #88. Several pathological small inputs made the pilot search hang (#14, #67, #87; the maintainer reports these as fixed). The author says MPHFs are meant for at least hundreds of thousands of keys.

When you need order preservation or membership tests. Output slots come in arbitrary order, and a key outside the build set still returns a valid-looking slot in [0, n), so you must store and compare keys yourself.

32-bit, embedded or MSVC/Windows targets. The author says it is meant for 64-bit architectures, and the code relies on __uint128_t and POSIX sysconf. Also, PHOBIC's dense_partitioned_phf cannot yet be built in external memory (open issue #90).

integration.dependencies: Header-only git submodules: jermp/bits (which pulls in jermp/essentials), jermp/mm_file and xxHash (included inline via xxh3.h). Also pthreads via CMake Threads::Threads. cmd_line_parser is used only by the bundled build/example tools.
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (C++14 is explicitly unsupported, per issue #8) and CMake >= 3.5. CI builds with GCC 11-14 and Clang 16-18 on Ubuntu 24.04; the paper used GCC 9.2.1.
integration.platforms: 64-bit only. Tested on Linux/GCC and macOS/Clang, on both x86-64 and Apple ARM (the author reports faster queries on M1 than on the x86 box). On x86-64 Unix, the CMake target adds -march=native -mbmi2 -msse4.2. Windows/MSVC support is not documented.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Lookup (operator()) is a const method that mutates no state, so concurrent lookups on a built function appear safe. Construction is parallel internally via config.num_threads, and search throws if that exceeds std::thread::hardware_concurrency().
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it fills the same role as BBHash (a static MPHF mapping keys to [0, n)), but the API is different: template-configured types, iterator plus build_configuration construction, and its own serialization. Call sites and saved files must be rewritten.

gotchas: build_configuration defaults to verbose=true, and seed-retry messages go to std::cout regardless, so set config.verbose=false in library code. The default seed is random (up to 10 retries), so builds are not reproducible unless you set config.seed. With a fixed seed, a failed search throws seed_runtime_error instead of retrying.
Duplicate keys, or colliding 64-bit hashes, make construction throw 'seed did not work'. The xxhash_64 hasher throws outright above 2^30 keys; use xxhash_128 for large sets.
The exported PTHASH CMake target injects -march=native into every consumer target on x86-64 Unix. Binaries built this way may not run on older CPUs; override the flags if you ship binaries.

The API and parameters changed after the benchmarked version. mphf_benchmark pins a Dec-2022 commit (b9a0c37) that uses the old 'c' parameter and MurmurHash2, while current master uses 'lambda', xxHash and a Bucketer template argument. Use release v2.0.0 to get 'c' semantics, and re-tune rather than copying the paper's configurations.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick PTHash when lookup latency dominates. In the same 1B-key table it answers in 37-101 ns/key, versus 199 ns for emphf and 197-220 ns for RecSplit, at a cost of roughly 0.4-1.4 bits/key more than RecSplit's 1.80. Prefer RecSplit, ShockHash or ConsensusRecSplit when you need to get down near 1.5-1.8 bits/key, and LPHash for k-mer sets (the PTHash author himself points k-mer users there).
verified_claims_summary: On the authors' mphf_benchmark harness (1 billion uniformly random 64-bit keys, single core, gcc 9.2.1 -O3 -march=native, Intel i9-9900K with 64 GB DDR3), PTHash looked up keys in 37 ns/key (C-C, 3.23 bits/key) and 55 ns/key (D-D, 2.99 bits/key), versus 170 ns/key for single-threaded BBHash gamma=1 (3.06 bits/key), about 3.1-4.6x faster. BBHash built the set faster (253 s versus 689-1042 s), and these numbers come from a 2022 PTHash commit, not the current lambda-based code.
status_note: Actively maintained: the last commit on 2026-07-27 added string_view keys and key mappers, and only one issue is open. It is MIT-licensed and header-only, and adding it as a git submodule is the documented integration path.
